# Introduction

## About Me & My Research

### Background

<p>
What makes a piece of music exciting? Could it be its tempo, valence, engagingness, danceability, instrumentalness, approachability, or the combination of some of them? 
</p>

<p>
In this portfolio, I intend to discover the factors that affect the arousal of a piece of music and how arousal is related to these factors. 
</p>

# Part I: Tempo and Valence

## Class Corpus Chart I Tempo-Arousal 

### Class Corpus Chart I Tempo-Arousal

```{r}
compmus2025 <- read_csv("compmus2025.csv")

compmus2025 |> ggplot(aes(x = tempo, y = arousal)) + geom_jitter() + geom_smooth()
```

### Findings: 

<p>
With Chart I, I intend to illustrate the relation between the tempo of a song and its arousal. 
</p>

<p>
Chart I indicates that the increase of tempo does not necessarily contribute to the increase of a song's arousal. Instead, it seems that most songs that sound more exciting and stimulating than others tend to have a tempo close to 100bpm. 
</p>

<p>
This means that there is a strong relation between valence and arousal.
</p>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Class Corpus Chart II Valence-Arousal

### Class Corpus Chart II Valence-Arousal

```{r}
compmus2025 |> ggplot(aes(x = valence, y = arousal)) + geom_jitter() + geom_smooth()
```

### Findings: 

<p>
With Chart II, I intend to illustrate the relation between the valence of a song and its arousal. 
</p>

<p>
Chart II indicates that the increase of valence does clearly contribute to the increase of a song's arousal. Indeed, it seems that the more positive and pleasant a piece of music sound, the more exciting and stimulating it would be. 
</p>


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


# Part II: Approachability and Instrumentalness

## Class Corpus Chart III

### Class Corpus Chart III Approachability-Arousal

```{r}
compmus2025 <- read_csv("compmus2025.csv")

library(plotly)

p <- compmus2025 |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = approachability,
      y = arousal,
      size = danceability,
      colour = valence,
      text = filename  # Add tooltip text
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_rug(linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(3, 7),
    breaks = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  scale_size_continuous(
    trans = "exp",
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    x = "Approachability",
    y = "Arousal",
    colour = "Valence"
  )

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
```

### Findings:

<p>
With Chart III, I intend to illustrate the relations between these factors: approachability, arousal, valence, and engagingness. According to Chart III, it is clear that with the increase in approachability, there does not occurs a similar change in arousal, valence, as well as engagingness, vice versa.  
</p>

<p>
Chart III indicates a weak relation between approachability and the other three features. More importantly, this means that whether or not a piece of music is exciting has very little to do with its approachability. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Class Corpus Chart IV

### Class Corpus Chart IV Instrumentalness-Arousal

```{r}
compmus2025 <- read_csv("compmus2025.csv")


# Create an interactive plot with song titles as tooltips
library(plotly)

p <- compmus2025 |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = instrumentalness,
      y = arousal,
      size = danceability,
      colour = valence,
      text = filename  # Add tooltip text
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_rug(linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(3, 7),
    breaks = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  scale_size_continuous(
    trans = "exp",
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    x = "Instrumentalness",
    y = "Arousal",
    colour = "Valence"
  )

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") # Convert to interactive plot with tooltips
```

### Findings:
<p>
With Chart IV, I intend to illustrate the relations between these factors: instrumentalness, arousal, valence, and danceability. According to Chart IV, it is clear that with the increase in instrumentalness, there occurs a decrease in arousal, valence, as well as danceability, vice versa. 
</p>

# Chart VII and Conclusion on Part I, II, and III

## Class Corpus Chart VII

### Class Corpus Chart VII Valence-Arousal
```{r}
compmus2025 <- read_csv("compmus2025.csv")

p <- compmus2025 |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = valence,
      y = arousal,
      size = engagingness,

    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_rug(linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(3, 7),

  ) +

    limits = c(3, 7),
    breaks = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  scale_size_continuous(
    trans = "exp",
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    x = "Valence",
    y = "Arousal",
    colour = "Danceability"
  )

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
```

### Findings: 

With Chart VII, I intend to illustrate the relations between these factors: valence, arousal, engagingness, and danceability. According to Chart VII, it is clear that with the increase in valence, there occurs an increase in arousal, engagingness, as well as danceability, vice versa. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


## conclusion

### Conclusion: 

<p>
In conclusion, based on Chart I-VII, it is clear that of all factors, engagingness, danceability, instrumentalness, and valence seem to have strong relations with the arousal of a piece of music, while the tempo of the music and its approachability does not have, generally saying, a positive or negative impact on the song's arousal. 
</p>

<p>
Therefore, what makes a song exciting? According to all the songs selected into compmus2025, we can conclude that if a piece of music sounds happier, catchier, and easier to dance to, it might sound more stimulating and exciting than other songs. Additionally, the amount of instrumental content in a piece of song may affect its arousal negatively, as it turns out with the increase of instrumentalness there comes a decrease in the arousal of the music.
</p>

# Valence and Arousal 

## Introduction 

### Introduction: 

<p>
As illustrated previously, valence has a strong connection with arousal. How does this work? What does it mean <i>musically</i> that one song has more valence than others? 
</p>

<p>
In this section, I will look into songs that have a higher valence than others and these songs musical features such as which chord they use which key they are in, their structre and variation, in order to better understand how valence contributes to a song's arousal. 
</p>

<p>

## Example I: reinout-w-2

### Example I (a): reinout-w-2 Chromagram

```{r}
"features/reinout-w-2.json" |>                           # Change the track
  compmus_chroma(norm = "identity") |>                 # Change the norm
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = pc, fill = value)) + 
  geom_raster() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 0:11,
    minor_breaks = NULL,
    labels = c(
                "C", "C#|Db", "D", "D#|Eb",
                "E", "F", "F#|Gb", "G",
                "G#|Ab", "A", "A#|Bb", "B"
              )
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +               # Change the colours?
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_classic()                                      # Change the theme?
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Example I (b): reinout-w-2 Chordogram
```{r}
"features/reinout-w-2.json" |> 
  compmus_chroma(norm = "identity") |> 
  compmus_match_pitch_templates(
    chord_templates,         # Change to chord_templates if desired
    norm = "identity",       # Try different norms (and match it with what you used in `compmus_chroma`)
    distance = "cosine"   # Try different distance metrics
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = name, fill = d)) + 
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +               # Change the colours?
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Template", fill = NULL) +
  theme_classic()                                      # Change the theme?
```
